source.title: Controlled Decoding Attacks on Black-Box LLMs
source.authors: Jesson Wang; Shawn Li; Wei Yang; Franck Dernoncourt; Ryan A. Rossi; C. Peris; Yue Zhao

page_placements.theme: Opening-token and sparse decoding interventions change safety

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper builds and evaluates its own sample-only controlled-decoding jailbreak, motivated in part by cited work on shallow alignment. It reports the performance of that attack and its components, rather than testing the underlying claims about fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base KL by response position, compliant-prefix prefilling, localized safety parameters, or deepening alignment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior findings about shallow alignment and compliant prefixes but supplies no new prefilling, suffix, or aligned-versus-base KL experiment. Figure 2 measures KL before and after this paper's intervention along successful attack trajectories, not between aligned and base models. Values used to select settings and cited results are not recorded as rows. Rows below record this paper's harmful-response scores for its controlled-decoding attack and its variants; they do not establish the broader claims in the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a sample-only controlled-decoding jailbreak (BlindBias) and reports only its own attack scores, ablations and cost trade-offs. It cites Qi et al. 2025 on shallow alignment as motivation. It never measures refusal without its intervention, never isolates the opening tokens (no first-k-only intervention versus later-position ablation), and runs no prefilling, fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base KL, parameter-localization or deepening experiment. Figure 2 KL compares the target before and after the paper's own intervention, not aligned versus base models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also conclude that withholding numerical probabilities alone may not close the decoding-time attack surface when repeated sampling and prefix continuation are allowed.
record.recipe_differences: A new sample-only controlled-decoding attack using reconstructed distributions, a prefix-risk gate, and speculative drafts; it is not a reproduction of either named original source. It adapts a separate cited BiasNet method to sampled-text access.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack scores vary by target, benchmark, evaluation metric, reconstruction prior, proxy prior, and gating pipeline. The authors also note that predictive fit and steering utility do not always track each other.

fits_no_version.finding: Along successful attack trajectories, the intervention-induced KL is small at most positions, with occasional large shifts (Figure 2, GLM-5 and Qwen3-32B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoding-time jailbreak interventions need large distribution shifts at only a few response positions, not necessarily the first ones.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemini-3.5-Flash, intervening at 5.25% of positions keeps most of the ungated attack's harm (Harm 3.58 vs 3.96).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse, prefix-conditioned decoding interventions retain most jailbreak effectiveness at much lower query cost.

record.problems: Attack scores are evaluated by Gemini-3.5-Flash; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper states that gains vary across targets and metrics. The KL result is shown in Figure 2 without numeric values in the text and measures the paper's intervention, not aligned-versus-base distributions. The gate-aware training diagnostics say that evaluation weights and support differ across rules and do not isolate training effects on common evaluation support.
record.rows_left_out: Prompt-level baseline attack scores in Table 1 are not rows because those methods do not use the decoding intervention at issue. Reconstruction predictive metrics and intervention-frequency/API-call metrics are omitted because they do not measure harmful compliance or a listed claim version. Table 5 gate-training margin and beats-base results are omitted because they are not harmful-compliance rates and have differing evaluation support.

untested.parts: No harmful-data fine-tuning. The LLM-LAT harmful data trains the external BiasNet controller, not the target.

Its own attack uses prefix continuation, but there is no no-attack refusal baseline and no prefill-only or opening-tokens-only condition. The attack's success cannot be attributed to getting past the opening.
No test of why alignment is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 reports no unattacked or prefill-only baseline, so the target's refusal rate without intervention is unknown. Harm scores are judged by Gemini-3.5-Flash, which is also a target, and no uncertainty is reported. The model names and dates are unusual (Gemini-3.5-Flash, GLM-5, an arXiv date in 2026); treat them as given.

versions.untested_parts: No per-position KL comparison between aligned and base models on harmful prompts; Figure 2 instead compares distributions before and after this paper's intervention.
The paper evaluates its own controlled-decoding attack, but does not test compliant-prefix prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as a general claim about bypassing refusal.
No experiment localizing safety to weights, ranks, or a small parameter set.
No experiment testing why safety alignment would be shallow.
No experiment deepening safety alignment or testing its durability.

relation.reason: The method uses prior findings about opening-token refusal and compliant prefixes to motivate selective intervention, while reporting its own controller's performance rather than independently testing a claim version.

tranche.reason: Shallow alignment motivates selective control; the experiments evaluate BlindBias attack performance, reconstruction and execution costs. Figure 2 compares distributions before and after attack intervention, rather than aligned and base models, and Table 4 compares complete attack pipelines without isolating opening-token sufficiency.

source_check.notes: These six rows are method-performance comparisons, not independent evidence for a claim version. The 5.25% measures BiasNet invocation frequency across positions; it does not identify a fixed opening window, and the pipeline comparison also changes controller training.
